LEAP: Accelerating ODE-based Diffusion Sampling with Optimal Linear Leaps

Conference: Proceedings of the 34th ACM International Conference on Multimedia; November 10–14, 2026; Rio de Janeiro, BrazilProceedings of the 34th ACM International Conference on Multimedia (MM ’26), November 10–14, 2026, Rio de Janeiro, BrazilDOI: 10.1145/3767308.3836106ISBN: 979-8-4007-2213-4/2026/11CCS: Computing methodologies Computer vision

Abstract.

Diffusion models primarily rely on general-purpose ODE-based numerical methods for training-free accelerated sampling, but performance degrades with coarse time discretization. In this paper, we propose optimal linear leaps (LEAP), a specialized method grounded in theoretical and empirical investigations of sampling trajectory geometry. Built upon low-dimensionality and cross-trajectory consistency, LEAP formulates a supervised least-squares optimization problem within the local trajectory subspace, achieving a precise approximation of future states without model evaluations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LEAP outperforms previous methods across diverse modalities, including text-to-image (Stable Diffusion 3.5, FLUX.1-dev) and image-to-3D (TRELLIS.2) generation. Furthermore, LEAP can be seamlessly integrated into existing solver-based methods, offering a plug-and-play enhancement for modern diffusion models. Code is available at https://github.com/zju-pi/LEAP.

Keywords: 
Diffusion Models, Training-free Acceleration, Solver-based
††cc-license: by

1. Introduction

Diffusion-based generative models (Ho et al., 2020; Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015; Song and Ermon, 2020; Song et al., 2020b) have achieved unprecedented success in multimedia content synthesis, ranging from image (Rombach et al., 2022; Ramesh et al., 2022; Saharia et al., 2022), video (Ho et al., 2022; Blattmann et al., 2023), audio (Kong et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2020), and 3D (Xiang et al., 2025; Hunyuan3D et al., 2025). Despite their remarkable generation quality, the slow sampling process imposes a critical bottleneck for latency-sensitive applications.

To address this issue, numerous acceleration techniques have been proposed. Training-based approaches distill a pre-trained multi-step model into an extremely few-step student model (Salimans and Ho, 2022; Luo et al., 2023; Song et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2023). However, distilling modern diffusion models with billions of parameters (e.g., 8B Stable Diffusion 3.5 (Esser et al., 2024) and 12B FLUX (Black Forest Labs, 2024)) is challenging and inflexible to accommodate community-tuned variants and LoRA modules. In contrast, training-free methods require minimal parameter updates, offering superior plug-and-play flexibility. Recent progress includes (i) solver-based method for calculating ordinary differential equations (ODEs) (Lu et al., 2022; Song et al., 2020a; Zhao et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2022a; Zhou et al., 2024), (ii) optimized timestep scheduling (Chen et al., 2025; Xue et al., 2024; Sabour et al., 2024), and (iii) feature caching (Ma et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2025; Wimbauer et al., 2024). Existing high-order multi-step solvers (Liu et al., 2022a; Lu et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2023) estimate future states via a linear combination of historical states where the coefficients are derived from numerical analysis, assuming sufficiently small and near-uniform step sizes. However, practical acceleration typically employs large and non-uniform step sizes, making their assumptions and associated convergence guarantees less reliable. Concurrently, emerging research on the geometric regularity of diffusion trajectories (Chen et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025; Wan et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2024) has uncovered intriguing empirical patterns, such as cross-trajectory consistency and low-dimensional concentration. While previous studies have qualitatively observed these regularities, a rigorous mathematical foundation remains largely absent. To move beyond heuristic designs toward a principled approach, a deeper and more rigorous investigation into the underlying mechanics is essential.

To bridge this gap, we conduct a comprehensive theoretical analysis of the geometric properties inherent in diffusion trajectories, yielding the following two theoretical insights. Firstly, we establish a theoretical bound on the alignment error between trajectories after orthogonal rotational alignment, revealing the cross-trajectory consistency of diffusion models. Secondly, we rigorously characterize the intrinsic low-dimensionality of diffusion sampling trajectories, proving that individual paths are confined to a low-dimensional subspace. Our analysis reveals that despite different noise initializations, these generative paths share consistent low-dimensional dynamics.

Leveraging these two mathematically grounded priors, we propose optimal linear leaps (LEAP), a training-free, solver-based acceleration framework. In contrast to traditional numerical solvers that rely on rigid Taylor coefficients, our method introduces a data-driven multi-step strategy powered by least-squares optimization. The intrinsic low-dimensionality of diffusion trajectories suggests that local path segments can be accurately characterized by a linear subspace. Leveraging this geometric regularity, we formulate the prediction as a least-squares optimization problem, which identifies the optimal linear coefficients by minimizing the discrepancy between linearly extrapolated historical states and multi-step ground-truth trajectory samples. Motivated by the cross-trajectory consistency, we demonstrate that the optimal linear extrapolation coefficients are sample-agnostic. This property guarantees the transferability of coefficients derived from a limited set of reference trajectories before inference, bypassing the overhead for per-sample optimization. LEAP significantly enhances the sampling efficiency while preserving high generation quality. Crucially, as it operates entirely at the macroscopic trajectory level, our approach functions as a model-agnostic and plug-and-play module. This allows for seamless integration into diverse diffusion models without any architectural modifications. Extensive experiments across diverse modalities, including text-to-image generation and text-to-3D generation demonstrate the superior performance and versatility of our method.

In summary, our main contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We prove the intrinsic low-dimensionality and geometric isomorphism of generative trajectories across diverse noise initializations.

  • •

    Motivated by these theoretical insights, we propose LEAP, a novel multi-step ODE solver that leverages least-squares alignment to learn sample-agnostic extrapolation coefficients, enabling highly accurate linear leaps with minimal computational overhead.

  • •

    Extensive experiments across diverse generative tasks that spanning both text-to-tmage synthesis and complex image-to-3D generation demonstrate the effectiveness of our method compared to state-of-the-art training-free baselines.

2. Preliminary

Diffusion Models. Continuous-time diffusion models progressively corrupt data 𝐱0∼pd​a​t​a​(𝐱)\mathbf{x}_{0}\sim p_{data}(\mathbf{x}) into a tractable noise distribution 𝐱T∼pp​r​i​o​r​(𝐱)\mathbf{x}_{T}\sim p_{prior}(\mathbf{x}) via a forward Stochastic Differential Equation (SDE) (Song et al., 2020b):

(1) d​𝐱t=f⁡(t)​𝐱t​d​t+g⁡(t)​d​𝐰t,t∈[0,T],\mathrm{d}\mathbf{x}_{t}=f(t)\mathbf{x}_{t}\mathrm{d}t+g(t)\mathrm{d}\mathbf{w}_{t},\qquad t\in[0,T],

where 𝐰t\mathbf{w}_{t} is the standard Wiener process (Oksendal, 2013), while f⁡(t)f(t) and g⁡(t)g(t) denote the drift and diffusion coefficients. Crucially, the generative process that reverses the forward SDE to recover the data distribution is governed by the reverse-time SDE d​𝐱t=[f⁡(t)​𝐱t−g​(t)2​∇𝐱t​log⁡pt​(𝐱t)]​d​t+g⁡(t)​d​𝐰¯t\mathrm{d}\mathbf{x}_{t}=[f(t)\mathbf{x}_{t}-g(t)^{2}\nabla_{\mathbf{x}_{t}}\log p_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})]\mathrm{d}t+g(t)\mathrm{d}\bar{\mathbf{w}}_{t}, where 𝐰¯t\bar{\mathbf{w}}_{t} denotes a standard Wiener process in the reverse-time direction. To implement the generative process, diffusion models estimate the intractable score function ∇𝐱t​log​pt​(𝐱t)\nabla_{\mathbf{x}_{t}}\log p_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}) using a neural network sθ​(𝐱t,t)s_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t) trained by score matching objectives. For any diffusion SDE, there exists an Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE) (Song et al., 2020b) that shares the identical marginal distributions pt​(𝐱)p_{t}(\mathbf{x}) for all t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T], which is known as the Probability Flow ODE (PF-ODE):

(2) d​𝐱t=[f⁡(t)​𝐱t−12​g​(t)2​∇𝐱t​log⁡pt​(𝐱t)]​d​t.\mathrm{d}\mathbf{x}_{t}=\left[f(t)\mathbf{x}_{t}-\frac{1}{2}g(t)^{2}\nabla_{\mathbf{x}_{t}}\log p_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})\right]\mathrm{d}t.

By casting the generative process as a numerical initial value problem, PF-ODE enables deterministic sampling and underpins various training-free solver-based acceleration methods (Lu et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2023).

Flow-based Models. Instead of explicitly defining a diffusion process through an SDE, flow-based generative models formulate a continuous-time Normalizing Flow (Lipman et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2022b; Albergo and Vanden-Eijnden, 2022). These models learn a time-dependent vector field v⁡(𝐱t,t)v(\mathbf{x}_{t},t) that transports noise to the data distribution via a deterministic ODE:

(3) d​𝐱t=v⁡(𝐱t,t)​d​t.\mathrm{d}\mathbf{x}_{t}=v(\mathbf{x}_{t},t)\mathrm{d}t.

To circumvent the direct estimation of intractable marginal vector fields, Flow Matching introduces a simulation-free objective which regresses a neural vector field vθ​(𝐱t,t)v_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t) towards a conditional vector field 𝐮t​(𝐱t|𝐱0)\mathbf{u}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}|\mathbf{x}_{0}) that defines the target probability path pt​(𝐱)p_{t}(\mathbf{x}):

(4) 𝔼t,p0​(𝐱0),pt​(𝐱t∣𝐱0)​[‖vθ​(𝐱t,t)−𝐮t​(𝐱t∣𝐱0)‖22].\mathbb{E}_{t,p_{0}(\mathbf{x}_{0}),p_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{0})}\left[\left\|v_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t)-\mathbf{u}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{0})\right\|_{2}^{2}\right].

Specifically, by setting T=1T=1, analytically solving Eq. 1 yields a reparameterization of 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t} as

(5) 𝐱t=αt​𝐱0+σt​𝐱1,𝐱1∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝐈).\mathbf{x}_{t}=\alpha_{t}\mathbf{x}_{0}+\sigma_{t}\mathbf{x}_{1},\qquad\mathbf{x}_{1}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}).

where

(6) αt=exp(∫0tf(u)du),σt=(∫0tg(u)2exp(−2∫0uf(s)ds)du)1/2.\small\alpha_{t}=\exp\left(\int_{0}^{t}f(u)\mathrm{d}u\right),\hskip 9.24994pt\sigma_{t}=\left(\int_{0}^{t}g(u)^{2}\exp\left(-2\int_{0}^{u}f(s)\mathrm{d}s\right)\mathrm{d}u\right)^{1/2}.

The conditional velocity field is thus given by

(7) 𝐮t​(𝐱t∣𝐱0)=σ˙tσt​𝐱t+(α˙t−αt​σ˙tσt)​𝐱0.\mathbf{u}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{0})=\frac{\dot{\sigma}_{t}}{\sigma_{t}}\mathbf{x}_{t}+\left(\dot{\alpha}_{t}-\alpha_{t}\frac{\dot{\sigma}_{t}}{\sigma_{t}}\right)\mathbf{x}_{0}.

Contemporary cutting-edge text-to-image models increasingly favor the Flow Matching framework due to its conceptual simplicity and flexible path design (Esser et al., 2024; Black Forest Labs, 2024). Since they inherit the architecture and training conventions of diffusion models, we still refer to the flow-based formulation as “diffusion” when no ambiguity arises.

Trajectory Regularity. While diffusion models operate in an immensely high-dimensional ambient space, recent empirical observations reveal that their sampling trajectories exhibit remarkable geometric regularity (Chen et al., 2024; Wang and Vastola, 2023; Chen et al., 2025). Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on individual sampling trajectory exhibits that the generative dynamics are inherently low-dimensional where the explained variance is dominated by the first few principal components. Furthermore, as illustrated in Fig. 2, when projecting multiple trajectories with distinct noise and prompt initializations into a shared 3D space, they bundle into a smooth ‘tube’. This visual alignment highlights a striking cross-trajectory consistency, indicating that different diffusion paths share nearly isomorphic macroscopic dynamics. Together, this inter-trajectory low-dimensionality and inter-trajectory consistency constitute the trajectory regularity, serving as the foundational intuition for our subsequent theoretical analysis and the design of our acceleration algorithm.

3. Methodology

3.1. The Intrinsic Geometry of Generative Trajectories

While previous works (Chen et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025) have observed strong geometric regularity of ODE sampling trajectories to justify existing accelerated sampling methods, a theoretical understanding remains unclear. In this section, we prove that diffusion sampling trajectories can be effectively aligned through orthogonal transformation and are embedded in low-dimensional subspaces. To this end, we perform an analysis within the Gaussian mixture model (GMM) framework with shared spherical covariance to analytically characterize diffusion dynamics. Since GMMs are universal approximators capable of modeling highly complex data manifolds, this assumption not only facilitates closed-form mathematical derivations but also ensures the broad applicability of our theoretical findings. Under this mild assumption, the data distribution is given by

(8) pdata​(𝐱)=∑s=1Sπs​𝒩​(𝝁s,σ02​𝐈d),πs>0,∑r=1Sπs=1,p_{\text{data}}(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{s=1}^{S}\pi_{s}\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{s},\sigma_{0}^{2}\mathbf{I}_{d}),\quad\pi_{s}>0,\quad\sum_{r=1}^{S}\pi_{s}=1,

where SS is the number of components, πs\pi_{s} are the mixing weights and 𝝁s\boldsymbol{\mu}_{s} are the cluster means. Let

U:=span⁡{𝝁1,…,𝝁S},r:=dim(U),R:=max1≤s≤S⁡‖𝝁s‖.U:=\operatorname{span}\{\boldsymbol{\mu}_{1},\dots,\boldsymbol{\mu}_{S}\},\quad r:=\dim(U),\quad R:=\max_{1\leq s\leq S}\|\boldsymbol{\mu}_{s}\|.

We consider the exact PF-ODE associated with the variance-preserving forward diffusion. Let t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T] denote the standard forward diffusion time. Denote 𝐱t(m)\mathbf{x}_{t}^{(m)} the mm-th sampling trajectory evolving backward in time which is initialized from a pure noise state 𝐱T(m)∼pT\mathbf{x}_{T}^{(m)}\sim p_{T}. which represents the displacement from the initial noise. Let

(10) αT:=exp(−12∫0Tβ(s)ds),νT2:=αT2σ02+(1−αT2).\alpha_{T}:=\exp\!\Big(-\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{T}\beta(s)\,ds\Big),\qquad\nu_{T}^{2}:=\alpha_{T}^{2}\sigma_{0}^{2}+(1-\alpha_{T}^{2}).

Suppose that 𝐱T(1),…,𝐱T(M)\mathbf{x}_{T}^{(1)},\dots,\mathbf{x}_{T}^{(M)} are i.i.d. samples from the exact noised marginal pTp_{T}. Then for every δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta,

uniformly over mm with high probability. Combining these bounds yields Thm. 3.1, and Cor. 3.2 follows by normalization with νT​d\nu_{T}\sqrt{d}.∎

Under the assumptions of Thm. 3.1, for each sampling trajectory 𝐱t(m)\mathbf{x}_{t}^{(m)}, there exists a linear subspace

For any fixed unit vector 𝐞∈U⟂\mathbf{e}\in U^{\perp}, there exist orthogonal matrices 𝐇1,…,𝐇M∈O⁡(d)\mathbf{H}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{H}_{M}\in O(d) satisfying 𝐇m|U=𝐈\mathbf{H}_{m}|_{U}=\mathbf{I} and

Under such transformations, the aligned trajectories defined by

(20) 𝐱¯tn(m):=𝐇m​𝐱tn(m)\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t_{n}}^{(m)}:=\mathbf{H}_{m}\mathbf{x}_{t_{n}}^{(m)}

all reside in the same (r+1)(r+1)-dimensional subspace

(21) 𝒮¯:=U⊕span⁡{𝐞}.\bar{\mathcal{S}}:=U\oplus\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf{e}\}.

PF-ODE exhibits two complementary structural properties: cross-trajectory consistency and intrinsic individual low-dimensionality. Thm. 3.1 establishes that, different sampling trajectories can be highly aligned through simple orthogonal transformation. Cor. 3.3 further demonstrates that each trajectory is strictly confined to an (r+1)(r+1)-dimensional subspace. Notably, after a simple per-trajectory alignment introduced by Cor. 3.4, the entire collection of trajectories resides within a universal (r+1)(r+1)-dimensional subspace. Therefore, the high-dimensional sampling dynamics are effectively governed by only a few latent coordinates: one radial coordinate in U⟂U^{\perp} and at most rr coordinates within the mean subspace UU.

More importantly, the intrinsic low-dimensionality established in Cor. 3.3 implies that, within any local window of a given trajectory, both the historical scores and the target output reside in a subspace. While this geometric regularity is rigorously established under mild assumption, its validity in real-world generative scenarios warrants empirical verification. To bridge this gap, we investigate the local score dynamics using sampling trajectories from Stable Diffusion 3.5. Specifically, we quantify the orthogonal projection error of the current score 𝐬t\mathbf{s}_{t} onto the local subspace spanned by a short historical buffer, denoted as span​(𝐬t+r,𝐬t+r−1,…,𝐬t+1)\text{span}(\mathbf{s}_{t+r},\mathbf{s}_{t+r-1},\ldots,\mathbf{s}_{t+1}). As illustrated in Fig. 3, the relative projection error is strictly bounded, dropping to a mere 4%–5% even with a small window size r=3r=3. This empirical finding confirms that even for highly complex data distributions, the immediate future score remains strictly confined within the linear span of its recent history. This empirical evident for low-dimensionality seamlessly transforms our theoretical insights into a practical algorithm, leading to our linear extrapolation framework in the subsequent section.

3.2. Optimal Linear Leaps with Aligned Trajectories

In this section, we present our method grounded in the the local linear dependence established above. This geometric regularity underpins the use of a linear extrapolator to predict next score function. The overall pipeline of our approach is illustrated in Fig. 1. To formalize this process, suppose we collect an ensemble of MM fine-grained reference sampling trajectories. For the mm-th trajectory (m=1,…,Mm=1,\ldots,M), denote 𝐬~n(m)\tilde{\mathbf{s}}_{n}^{(m)} the model output (e.g., estimated score function) at timestep tnt_{n}, and let 𝐱~n−1(m)\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{n-1}^{(m)} be the next state updated using 𝐬~n(m)\tilde{\mathbf{s}}_{n}^{(m)}.

Given a window size rr, our objective at timestep tnt_{n} is to predict the next model output 𝐬~n−1\tilde{\mathbf{s}}_{n-1} by utilizing rr stored previous model outputs along the sampling trajectory. Denote the local history matrix of scores and the corresponding target by

(22) 𝐇n(m)=[𝐬~n+r−1(m),𝐬~n+r−2(m),…,𝐬~n(m)]∈ℝd×r.\mathbf{H}_{n}^{(m)}=\left[\tilde{\mathbf{s}}_{n+r-1}^{(m)},\tilde{\mathbf{s}}_{n+r-2}^{(m)},\ldots,\tilde{\mathbf{s}}_{n}^{(m)}\right]\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r}.

We seek an optimal coefficient vector 𝐰n∈ℝr\mathbf{w}_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{r} that satisfies:

(23) 𝐬~n−1(m)≈𝐇n(m)​𝐰n.\tilde{\mathbf{s}}_{n-1}^{(m)}\approx\mathbf{H}_{n}^{(m)}\mathbf{w}_{n}.

The cross-trajectory consistency presented in Thm. 3.1 demonstrates that, after proper alignment, different trajectories follow nearly isomorphic low-dimensional dynamics. Consequently, a single coefficient vector 𝐰n\mathbf{w}_{n} can effectively characterize the score evolution of different reference trajectories at a given sampling timestep, enabling the extraction of a universal local extrapolation law. Formally, we derive the step-wise optimal predictor within the family of linear extrapolators by solving the following multi-trajectory least-squares problem:

(24) 𝐰n⋆=arg⁡min⁡∑m=1M𝐰∈ℝr⁡‖𝐬~n−1(m)−𝐇n(m)​𝐰‖22.\mathbf{w}_{n}^{\star}=\arg\min_{\mathbf{w}\in\mathbb{R}^{r}}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\left\|\tilde{\mathbf{s}}_{n-1}^{(m)}-\mathbf{H}_{n}^{(m)}\mathbf{w}\right\|_{2}^{2}.

While the formulation above is conceptually straightforward, directly regressing on [𝐬~n+r−1,𝐬~n+r−2,…,𝐬~n][\tilde{\mathbf{s}}_{n+r-1},\tilde{\mathbf{s}}_{n+r-2},\ldots,\tilde{\mathbf{s}}_{n}] is often numerically ill-posed. Since consecutive model outputs along smooth segments of the diffusion path are highly correlated, the columns of the history matrix tend to be nearly collinear. As a result, the associated least-squares system becomes poorly conditioned, making the fitted coefficients sensitive to finite-sample error, imperfect cross-trajectory alignment, and numerical instabilities. To mitigate this issue, we reparameterize the local subspace using a difference basis rather than the raw basis. Specifically, for each trajectory window, we define the first-order differences of the scores as:

(25) Δn,j(m):=𝐬~n+j(m)−𝐬~n+j−1(m),j=1,…,r−1,\Delta_{n,j}^{(m)}:=\tilde{\mathbf{s}}_{n+j}^{(m)}-\tilde{\mathbf{s}}_{n+j-1}^{(m)},\qquad j=1,\ldots,r-1,

and define the modified history matrix as:

(26) 𝐁n(m)=[Δn,r−1(m),…,Δn,1(m),𝐬~n(m)]∈ℝd×r.\mathbf{B}_{n}^{(m)}=\left[\Delta_{n,r-1}^{(m)},\ldots,\Delta_{n,1}^{(m)},\tilde{\mathbf{s}}_{n}^{(m)}\right]\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r}.

Rather than directly estimating 𝐰n\mathbf{w}_{n}, we fit an auxiliary coefficient vector 𝐜n∈ℝr\mathbf{c}_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{r} such that

(27) 𝐬~n−1(m)≈𝐁n(m)​𝐜n.\tilde{\mathbf{s}}_{n-1}^{(m)}\approx\mathbf{B}_{n}^{(m)}\mathbf{c}_{n}.

In practice, we aggregate samples from all reference trajectories and solve a ridge regression problem within the difference basis for each timestep n=N−1,N−2,…,rn=N-1,N-2,\ldots,r:

(28) 𝐜n⋆=arg⁡min⁡∑m=1M𝐜∈ℝr⁡‖𝐬~n−1(m)−𝐁n(m)​𝐜‖22+λ​‖𝐜‖22.\mathbf{c}_{n}^{\star}=\arg\min_{\mathbf{c}\in\mathbb{R}^{r}}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\left\|\tilde{\mathbf{s}}_{n-1}^{(m)}-\mathbf{B}_{n}^{(m)}\mathbf{c}\right\|_{2}^{2}+\lambda\|\mathbf{c}\|_{2}^{2}.

Once the step-wise coefficient bank 𝒞={𝐜N−r+1,𝐜N−r,…,𝐜1}\mathcal{C}=\{\mathbf{c}_{N-r+1},\mathbf{c}_{N-r},\ldots,\mathbf{c}_{1}\} has been solved, inference proceeds in two phases. First, we execute a warm-up phase by running the initial rr denoising steps in a standard way. This initializes the history buffer with the initial rr model outputs and their corresponding states:

(29) {𝐬~N,𝐬~N−2,…,𝐬~N−r+1},{𝐱~N,𝐱~N−2,…,𝐱~N−r}.\{\tilde{\mathbf{s}}_{N},\tilde{\mathbf{s}}_{N-2},\ldots,\tilde{\mathbf{s}}_{N-r+1}\},\quad\{\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{N},\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{N-2},\ldots,\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{N-r}\}.

This warm-up phase provides the minimum context required by the extrapolator. Moving forward, we employ an interleaved sampling strategy that alternates between a network-free prediction step and a network-based correction step. Specifically, suppose the current history buffer contains rr most recent scores:

(30) {𝐬~n+r−1,𝐬~n+r−2,…,𝐬~n}.\{\tilde{\mathbf{s}}_{n+r-1},\tilde{\mathbf{s}}_{n+r-2},\ldots,\tilde{\mathbf{s}}_{n}\}.

We first predict the next model output using the learned step-wise coefficients:

(31) 𝐬^n−1:=𝐜n,r−1​𝐬~n+∑j=0r−2𝐜n,j​Δn,r−j−1.\hat{\mathbf{s}}_{n-1}:=\mathbf{c}_{n,r-1}\tilde{\mathbf{s}}_{n}+\sum_{j=0}^{r-2}\mathbf{c}_{n,j}\,\Delta_{n,r-j-1}.

The extrapolated score 𝐬^n−1\hat{\mathbf{s}}_{n-1} is then utilized to evolve the trajectory to 𝐱^n−2\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{n-2} via numerical solvers, eliminating the need for an explicit network evaluation. The extrapolated score 𝐬^n−1\hat{\mathbf{s}}_{n-1} then serves as a proxy for 𝐬~n−1\tilde{\mathbf{s}}_{n-1} and is pushed into the history buffer, displacing the oldest entry to maintain a fixed window size of rr.

Extrapolation alone inevitably accumulates numerical drift over time. To ensure trajectory stability, we implement an interleaved Predict-Correct scheme. Following the short warm-up stage, the solver alternates between network-free extrapolation and exact network evaluation, balancing computational efficiency with numerical robustness, providing a practical acceleration framework for diffusion sampling. Given the step-wise optimality of our linear extrapolators and their capability to bypass redundant network evaluations, we name our method as Optimal Linear Leaps (LEAP). The full algorithms of coefficient bank construction and LEAP sampling are provided in Algorithm 1 and 2.

4. Experiments

We evaluate the proposed LEAP on three cutting-edge diffusion models: SD3.5-Medium (Esser et al., 2024) and FLUX.1-Dev (Black Forest Labs, 2024) for text-image task and TRELLIS.2 (Xiang et al., 2025) for image-3D task. The quality of generated images is quantitatively evaluated using three metrics, including ImageReward (Xu et al., 2023), CLIP Score (Radford et al., 2021), and HPSv2 (Wu et al., 2023). The prompts are drawn from the DrawBench (Saharia et al., 2022) dataset. For image-3D task, we evaluate 3D object on a test set of 100 randomly sampled images from the Google Scanned Objects (GSO) dataset (Downs et al., 2022) by PSNR and CLIP Score. By default, we fix a window size of r=5r=5 and set the ridge regularization coefficient to λ=0.0001\lambda=0.0001 across all experiments. Unless otherwise specified, LEAP is compared with existing state-of-the-art solvers under identical inference settings.

4.1. Main Results

Text-to-image Generation. We evaluate LEAP on text-to-image generation, benchmarking it against representative solvers including Euler method (Song et al., 2020a), DPM++ (Lu et al., 2025), UniPC (Zhao et al., 2023), iPNDM (von Platen et al., 2022), LTC-Accel (Zhu et al., 2025) and STORK-4 (Tan et al., 2025). As shown in Tab. 1, LEAP consistently achieves top-tier performance across diverse sampling budgets, effectively preserving both text-image alignment and perceptual quality for accelerated sampling. Moreover, LEAP consistently enhances the performance of both first-order and higher-order solvers, demonstrating its versatile plug-and-play capability. By leveraging a pre-computed, step-wise coefficient bank, LEAP seamlessly adapts any solver without any solver-specific hyperparameter tuning or model fine-tuning, making it a solver-agnostic enhancement module. Fig. 4 provides a qualitative comparison of LEAP against state-of-the-art solvers on SD3.5-Medium. Our LEAP exhibits superior performance across four challenging scenarios including (1) text rendering: LEAP accurately synthesizes legible text, whereas baselines suffer from typographic errors; (2) physical lighting: LEAP captures realistic transparency and intricate light refraction; (3) attribute binding: LEAP precisely binds the localized attributes to their respective partitions without semantic leakage.

Image-to-3D Generation. We further validate LEAP on image-to-3D generation using the TRELLIS.2 (Xiang et al., 2025) architecture. As presented in Tab. 2, our method achieves systematic improvements in both PSNR and CLIP Score over the baseline on GSO dataset. The qualitative results shown in Fig. 5 demonstrate LEAP’s superior capability in (1) topological correctness, maintaining precise connectivity in complex jointed structures; (2) surface fidelity; (3) geometric completeness, effectively generating intricate and high-frequency geometries, yielding sharper textural details and superior color accuracy.

4.2. Ablation Study

To systematically validate the contribution of each key design choice in the proposed method, we conduct comprehensive ablation studies on SD3.5-Medium. To ensure a rigorous comparison, we isolate the impact of each component by maintaining a fixed NN-step sampling schedule, identical random seeds and a consistent ensemble of reference trajectory (default M=32M=32). (a) Window Size rr. As shown in Fig 6(a), we adopt r=5r=5 as the default window size, as it delivers peak or near-peak performance in most scenarios. (b) Penalty Strength λ\lambda. Fig. 6(b) demonstrates that LEAP is robust to the penalty coefficient λ\lambda across a wide range of values. We retain this penalty term across all experiments to ensure theoretical consistency and numerical stability. (c) Number of Reference Trajectories MM. As shown in Fig 6(c), LEAP exhibits remarkable data efficiency, maintaining high performance even with minimal reference data (M≤2M\leq 2). This observation perfectly corroborates our theoretical analysis regarding cross-trajectory consistency. We default to M=32M=32 to ensure statistically robust coverage across diverse prompts. (d) Basis Construction. Fig. 7 underscores the critical role of our difference-basis reparameterization. The difference basis effectively rectifies the ill-conditioning, ensuring numerical stability and enabling consistent quality improvements across all NFE settings.

5. Related Works

Fast numerical solvers. A predominant branch of training-free acceleration methods focuses on improving the numerical solver employed in reverse-time sampling. Early work such as DDIM (Song et al., 2020a) established the ODE-based paradigm for fast deterministic generation. Subsequent research has developed increasingly effective high-order and multi-step solvers. PNDM (Liu et al., 2022a) introduced multi-step pseudo numerical methods, showing that leveraging historical samples can significantly improve the quality-speed trade-off over first-order samplers. Its improved implementation, iPNDM (von Platen et al., 2022), is frequently utilized in modern diffusion sampling. DEIS (Zhang and Chen, 2022) further exploited the semi-linear structure of diffusion dynamics through an exponential-integrator formulation. Similarly, DPM-Solver (Lu et al., 2022) and DPM++ (Lu et al., 2025) derived dedicated high-order solvers by analytically isolating the linear components, significantly reducing discretization errors, and have emerged as a robust practical standard, particularly for guided sampling scenarios. UniPC (Zhao et al., 2023) unified the predictor-corrector paradigm. Subsequent refinements such as DPM-Solver-v3 (Zheng et al., 2023) and DC-Solver (Zhao et al., 2024), further improved solver parameterization and correction stability. LTC-Accel (Zhu et al., 2025) leverages the local transition coherence of generative trajectories to dynamically approximate adjacent network outputs, achieving training-free acceleration. STORK (Tan et al., 2025) addressed numerical stiffness and removed the reliance on semi-linear assumptions and proposed a stabilized solver. Despite their differences, these methods still construct update rules primarily from numerical analysis or step-wise trend heuristics. In contrast, our method revisits multi-step solving from a trajectory-geometric perspective and seeks to exploit the intrinsic low-dimensional and cross-trajectory consistent structure of generative trajectories more directly.

Diffusion sampling dynamics. Prior research on diffusion sampling dynamics has mainly established trajectory regularity through empirical observations, supported by preliminary theoretical insights under idealized settings. Notably, Wang et al. (Wang and Vastola, 2023) observed that individual reverse-time sampling trajectories are effectively low-dimensional, often resembling two-dimensional rotations. Chen et al. (Chen et al., 2024) studied deterministic PF-ODE trajectories, finding that each trajectory closely follows the displacement between its endpoints, with residuals neatly captured by two or three orthogonal directions, yielding a characteristic boomerang-like shape. Their subsequent work (Chen et al., 2025) strengthened the cross-trajectory consistency claim by aligning projected trajectories with orthogonal Procrustes, revealing a nearly canonical trajectory shape after sample-specific rotations and reflections. While these works have empirically uncovered the trajectory regularity of diffusion sampling dynamics, their theoretical grounding relies largely on KDE-based surrogates of the empirical data distribution, analytically tractable Gaussian models, and supportive Gaussian-mixture calculations. To the best of our knowledge, prior literature lacks a unified theorem within a Mixture-of-Gaussian framework that jointly formalizes both trajectory low-dimensionality and cross-trajectory isomorphism. In contrast, our work provides a principled derivation that simultaneously establishes these two properties.

6. Conclusion

In this paper, we introduced LEAP, a novel, training-free multi-step ODE solver that effectively addresses the performance degradation of diffusion models in low-NFE regimes. Our approach is built upon a rigorous investigation of the geometric properties of diffusion sampling trajectories. By proving the intrinsic low-dimensionality and cross-trajectory consistency of generative paths, we formulated a supervised least-squares optimization within the local trajectory subspace. This allows LEAP to derive optimal, sample-agnostic extrapolation coefficients, achieving accurate future state approximations with minimal computational overhead. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that LEAP serves as a versatile, plug-and-play enhancement for modern large-scale diffusion models. LEAP consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across diverse modalities, including text-to-image generation using Stable Diffusion 3.5 and FLUX.1-Dev and image-to-3D generation using TRELLIS.2. Future work will delve deeper into the geometric properties of diffusion sampling trajectories under practical settings to further align our theoretical framework with realistic, finite-step sampling scenarios.

Appendix A Proofs for Section 3.1

This appendix section proves Theorems and Corollaries from Section 3.1. First, we provide an exact decomposition of the PF-ODE under a mild assumption. Next, we prove the deterministic pairwise alignment bound. Finally, we apply the Gaussian concentration theorem to get a high-probability bound.

A.1. Notations

Consider the variance-preserving forward diffusion situation:

(32) d​𝐗t=−12​β​(t)​𝐗t​d​t+β⁡(t)​d​𝐖t,t∈[0,T],d\mathbf{X}_{t}=-\frac{1}{2}\beta(t)\mathbf{X}_{t}\,dt+\sqrt{\beta(t)}\,d\mathbf{W}_{t},\qquad t\in[0,T],

where β:[0,T]→(0,∞)\beta:[0,T]\to(0,\infty) is integrable. We define

(33) αt:=exp(−12∫0tβ(s)ds),νt2:=αt2σ02+(1−αt2).\alpha_{t}:=\exp\!\Big(-\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{t}\beta(s)\,ds\Big),\qquad\nu_{t}^{2}:=\alpha_{t}^{2}\sigma_{0}^{2}+(1-\alpha_{t}^{2}).

Suppose data distribution satisfies GMM assumption:

(34) p0​(𝐱)=∑m=1Mπm​𝒩​(𝝁m,σ02​𝐈d),πm>0,∑m=1Mπm=1.p_{0}(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{m=1}^{M}\pi_{m}\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{m},\sigma_{0}^{2}\mathbf{I}_{d}),\qquad\pi_{m}>0,\qquad\sum_{m=1}^{M}\pi_{m}=1.

To describe the layout of the mixed distribution center, we define the space formed by their means as

(35) U:=span⁡{𝝁1,…,𝝁M},r:=dim(U),R:=max1≤m≤M⁡‖𝝁m‖.U:=\operatorname{span}\{\boldsymbol{\mu}_{1},\dots,\boldsymbol{\mu}_{M}\},\qquad r:=\dim(U),\qquad R:=\max_{1\leq m\leq M}\|\boldsymbol{\mu}_{m}\|.

We also let PP to be the orthogonal projection onto UU, with Q:=𝐈−PQ:=\mathbf{I}-P.

A.2. Structural lemmas

We now begin to derive the closed-form expressions of PF-ODE dynamics. We start our proofs by formulating the marginal probability density of the forward diffusion.

Lemma A.1 (Closed Form of Marginal Probability Function).

For every t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T], we have

(36) pt​(𝐱)=∑s=1Sπs​𝒩​(αt​𝝁s,νt2​𝐈d).p_{t}(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{s=1}^{S}\pi_{s}\mathcal{N}(\alpha_{t}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{s},\nu_{t}^{2}\mathbf{I}_{d}).
Proof.

Suppose C∈{1,…,S}C\in\{1,\dots,S\} satisfy condition ℙ⁡(C=s)=πs\mathbb{P}(C=s)=\pi_{s}, and suppose the conditional probability density of the initial state is

(37) p⁡(𝐱0∣C=s)=𝒩⁡(𝐱0,𝝁s,σ02​𝐈d).p(\mathbf{x}_{0}\mid C=s)=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_{0};\boldsymbol{\mu}_{s},\sigma_{0}^{2}\mathbf{I}_{d}).

Because forward diffusion process defines the transition probability density:

(38) p⁡(𝐱t∣𝐱0)=𝒩⁡(𝐱t,αt​𝐱0,(1−αt2)​𝐈d).p(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{0})=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_{t};\alpha_{t}\mathbf{x}_{0},(1-\alpha_{t}^{2})\mathbf{I}_{d}).

Hence, conditional on C=sC=s, the probability density of 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t} is obtained by the following equation:

(39) p⁡(𝐱t∣C=s)\displaystyle p(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid C=s) =∫p⁡(𝐱t∣𝐱0)​p​(𝐱0∣C=s)​d​𝐱0\displaystyle=\int p(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{0})p(\mathbf{x}_{0}\mid C=s)\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{x}_{0}
=𝒩⁡(𝐱t,αt​𝝁s,(αt2​σ02+1−αt2)​𝐈d)\displaystyle=\mathcal{N}\!\bigl(\mathbf{x}_{t};\alpha_{t}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{s},(\alpha_{t}^{2}\sigma_{0}^{2}+1-\alpha_{t}^{2})\mathbf{I}_{d}\bigr)
=𝒩⁡(𝐱t,αt​𝝁s,νt2​𝐈d).\displaystyle=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_{t};\alpha_{t}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{s},\nu_{t}^{2}\mathbf{I}_{d}).

Averaging over ss gives the claim. ∎

Lemma A.2 (Closed-form of score function).

Define

(40) ws​(𝐱,t):=πs​exp⁡(αtνt2​⟨𝐱,𝝁s⟩−αt22​νt2​‖𝝁s‖2)∑j=1Sπj​exp⁡(αtνt2​⟨𝐱,𝝁j⟩−αt22​νt2​‖𝝁j‖2),w_{s}(\mathbf{x},t):=\frac{\pi_{s}\exp\!\Big(\frac{\alpha_{t}}{\nu_{t}^{2}}\langle\mathbf{x},\boldsymbol{\mu}_{s}\rangle-\frac{\alpha_{t}^{2}}{2\nu_{t}^{2}}\|\boldsymbol{\mu}_{s}\|^{2}\Big)}{\sum_{j=1}^{S}\pi_{j}\exp\!\Big(\frac{\alpha_{t}}{\nu_{t}^{2}}\langle\mathbf{x},\boldsymbol{\mu}_{j}\rangle-\frac{\alpha_{t}^{2}}{2\nu_{t}^{2}}\|\boldsymbol{\mu}_{j}\|^{2}\Big)},

and

(41) 𝐦t​(𝐱):=∑s=1Sws​(𝐱,t)​𝝁s.\mathbf{m}_{t}(\mathbf{x}):=\sum_{s=1}^{S}w_{s}(\mathbf{x},t)\boldsymbol{\mu}_{s}.

Then

(42) ∇log⁡pt​(𝐱)=−1νt2​(𝐱−αt​𝐦t​(𝐱)).\nabla\log p_{t}(\mathbf{x})=-\frac{1}{\nu_{t}^{2}}\bigl(\mathbf{x}-\alpha_{t}\mathbf{m}_{t}(\mathbf{x})\bigr).
Proof.

By Lemma A.1,

(43) pt​(𝐱)=∑s=1Sπs​ϕνt2​𝐈d​(𝐱−αt​𝝁s),p_{t}(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{s=1}^{S}\pi_{s}\phi_{\nu_{t}^{2}\mathbf{I}_{d}}(\mathbf{x}-\alpha_{t}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{s}),

where ϕ𝚺\phi_{\mathbf{\Sigma}} denotes the Gaussian density with covariance 𝚺\mathbf{\Sigma}. Therefore,

(44) ∇pt(𝐱)=−1νt2∑s=1Sπs(𝐱−αt𝝁s)ϕνt2​𝐈d(𝐱−αt𝝁s).\nabla p_{t}(\mathbf{x})=-\frac{1}{\nu_{t}^{2}}\sum_{s=1}^{S}\pi_{s}(\mathbf{x}-\alpha_{t}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{s})\phi_{\nu_{t}^{2}\mathbf{I}_{d}}(\mathbf{x}-\alpha_{t}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{s}).

Therefore, the closed-form of score function can be derived by dividing Eq. 44 by pt​(𝐱)p_{t}(\mathbf{x}):

(45) ∇log⁡pt​(𝐱)=−1νt2​(𝐱−αt​∑s=1Sws​(𝐱,t)​𝝁s)=−1νt2​(𝐱−αt​𝐦t​(𝐱)).\nabla\log p_{t}(\mathbf{x})=-\frac{1}{\nu_{t}^{2}}\Bigl(\mathbf{x}-\alpha_{t}\sum_{s=1}^{S}w_{s}(\mathbf{x},t)\boldsymbol{\mu}_{s}\Bigr)=-\frac{1}{\nu_{t}^{2}}\bigl(\mathbf{x}-\alpha_{t}\mathbf{m}_{t}(\mathbf{x})\bigr).

∎

Lemma A.3 (Sufficiency of Mean Subspace).

For every 𝐱∈ℝd\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T],

(46) ws​(𝐱,t)=ws​(P​𝐱,t),𝐦t​(𝐱)=𝐦t​(P​𝐱)∈U.w_{s}(\mathbf{x},t)=w_{s}(P\mathbf{x},t),\qquad\mathbf{m}_{t}(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{m}_{t}(P\mathbf{x})\in U.

Furthermore, let 𝐱t∈[0,T]\mathbf{x}_{t\in[0,T]} be a PF-ODE trajectory. Its derivative with respect to tt is given by

(47) d​𝐱td​t=at​𝐱t+bt​𝐦t​(P​𝐱t),\frac{d\mathbf{x}_{t}}{dt}=a_{t}\mathbf{x}_{t}+b_{t}\mathbf{m}_{t}(P\mathbf{x}_{t}),

where

(48) at:=12​β​(t)​(1−νt−2),bt:=12​β​(t)​αt​νt−2.a_{t}:=\frac{1}{2}\beta(t)\Bigl(1-\nu_{t}^{-2}\Bigr),\qquad b_{t}:=\frac{1}{2}\beta(t)\alpha_{t}\nu_{t}^{-2}.
Proof.

Note that the expression for ws​(𝐱,t)w_{s}(\mathbf{x},t) only depends on 𝐱\mathbf{x} through the inner products ⟨𝐱,𝝁s⟩\langle\mathbf{x},\boldsymbol{\mu}_{s}\rangle. Since for 𝝁s∈U\boldsymbol{\mu}_{s}\in U, we have

(49) ⟨𝐱,𝝁s⟩=⟨P​𝐱,𝝁s⟩,\langle\mathbf{x},\boldsymbol{\mu}_{s}\rangle=\langle P\mathbf{x},\boldsymbol{\mu}_{s}\rangle,

which leads to ws​(𝐱,t)=ws​(P​𝐱,t)w_{s}(\mathbf{x},t)=w_{s}(P\mathbf{x},t). Furthermore, it is obvious that 𝐦t​(x)∈U\mathbf{m}_{t}(x)\in U because it is simply a sum of vectors μs∈U\mu_{s}\in U:

(50) 𝐦t​(𝐱)=∑s=1Sws​(𝐱,t)​𝝁s.\mathbf{m}_{t}(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{s=1}^{S}w_{s}(\mathbf{x},t)\boldsymbol{\mu}_{s}.

In forward process, the PF-ODE is

(51) d​𝐱td​t\displaystyle\frac{d\mathbf{x}_{t}}{dt} =−12β(t)𝐱t−12β(t)∇logpt(𝐱t)\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2}\beta(t)\mathbf{x}_{t}-\frac{1}{2}\beta(t)\nabla\log p_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})
=12​β​(t)​[𝐱t−νt−2​𝐱t+αt​νt−2​𝐦t​(𝐱t)].\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\beta(t)\Bigl[\mathbf{x}_{t}-\nu_{t}^{-2}\mathbf{x}_{t}+\alpha_{t}\nu_{t}^{-2}\mathbf{m}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})\Bigr].

Using Eq. 46 immediately yields Eq.47. ∎

Lemma A.4 (Exact U⊕U⟂U\oplus U^{\perp} decomposition).

Let

(52) Φ⁡(t2,t1):=exp⁡(∫t1t2av​𝑑v),ρt:=Φ⁡(t,T).\Phi(t_{2},t_{1}):=\exp\!\Big(\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}a_{v}\,dv\Big),\qquad\rho_{t}:=\Phi(t,T).

Then we obtain the following equation by integrating from TT to tt:

(53) Q​𝐱t=ρt​Q​𝐱T,Q\mathbf{x}_{t}=\rho_{t}Q\mathbf{x}_{T},

and

(54) P​𝐱t=ρt​P​𝐱T−∫tTΦ⁡(t,τ)​bτ​𝐦τ​(P​𝐱τ)​𝑑τ.P\mathbf{x}_{t}=\rho_{t}P\mathbf{x}_{T}-\int_{t}^{T}\Phi(t,\tau)b_{\tau}\,\mathbf{m}_{\tau}(P\mathbf{x}_{\tau})\,d\tau.

As a result,

(55) Q​𝐃t=(ρt−1)​Q​𝐱T.Q\mathbf{D}_{t}=(\rho_{t}-1)Q\mathbf{x}_{T}.
Proof.

Apply QQ to Eq. 47. Since 𝐦t​(P​𝐱t)∈U\mathbf{m}_{t}(P\mathbf{x}_{t})\in U, we obtain

(56) Q​d​𝐱td​t=at​Q​𝐱t,Q\frac{d\mathbf{x}_{t}}{dt}=a_{t}Q\mathbf{x}_{t},

whose exact solution is

(57) Q​𝐱t=exp⁡(∫Ttav​𝑑v)​Q​𝐱T=ρt​Q​𝐱T.Q\mathbf{x}_{t}=\exp\!\Big(\int_{T}^{t}a_{v}\,dv\Big)Q\mathbf{x}_{T}=\rho_{t}Q\mathbf{x}_{T}.

Similarly, for the projection PP, we can obtain that

(58) P​d​𝐱td​t=at​P​𝐱t+bt​𝐦t​(P​𝐱t),P\frac{d\mathbf{x}_{t}}{dt}=a_{t}P\mathbf{x}_{t}+b_{t}\mathbf{m}_{t}(P\mathbf{x}_{t}),

and the variation-of-constants formula (integrating from TT to tt) leads to

(59) P​𝐱t=ρt​P​𝐱T+∫TtΦ⁡(t,τ)​bτ​𝐦τ​(P​𝐱τ)​𝑑τ.P\mathbf{x}_{t}=\rho_{t}P\mathbf{x}_{T}+\int_{T}^{t}\Phi(t,\tau)b_{\tau}\,\mathbf{m}_{\tau}(P\mathbf{x}_{\tau})\,d\tau.

Subtracting Q​𝐱TQ\mathbf{x}_{T} immediately gives the Eq. 55. ∎

Lemma A.5 (Mean-Subspace Displacement Bound).

Define

(60) AT:=sup0≤t≤T|ρt−1|,BT:=sup0≤t≤T∫tTΦ⁡(t,τ)​|bτ|​𝑑τ.A_{T}:=\sup_{0\leq t\leq T}|\rho_{t}-1|,\qquad B_{T}:=\sup_{0\leq t\leq T}\int_{t}^{T}\Phi(t,\tau)|b_{\tau}|\,d\tau.

Then every trajectory satisfies

(61) sup0≤t≤T‖P​𝐃t‖≤AT​‖P​𝐱T‖+BT​R.\sup_{0\leq t\leq T}\|P\mathbf{D}_{t}\|\leq A_{T}\|P\mathbf{x}_{T}\|+B_{T}R.
Proof.

By Lemma A.4,

(62) P​𝐃t=(ρt−1)​P​𝐱T−∫tTΦ⁡(t,τ)​bτ​𝐦τ​(P​𝐱τ)​𝑑τ.P\mathbf{D}_{t}=(\rho_{t}-1)P\mathbf{x}_{T}-\int_{t}^{T}\Phi(t,\tau)b_{\tau}\,\mathbf{m}_{\tau}(P\mathbf{x}_{\tau})\,d\tau.

Since 𝐦τ​(P​𝐱τ)\mathbf{m}_{\tau}(P\mathbf{x}_{\tau}) is a convex combination of 𝝁1,…,𝝁M\boldsymbol{\mu}_{1},\dots,\boldsymbol{\mu}_{M}, it’s obvious that

(63) ‖𝐦τ​(P​𝐱τ)‖≤R.\|\mathbf{m}_{\tau}(P\mathbf{x}_{\tau})\|\leq R.

Hence by using the triangle inequality, we have

(64) ‖P​𝐃t‖≤|ρt−1|​‖P​𝐱T‖+∫tTΦ⁡(t,τ)​|bτ|​R​𝑑τ.\|P\mathbf{D}_{t}\|\leq|\rho_{t}-1|\|P\mathbf{x}_{T}\|+\int_{t}^{T}\Phi(t,\tau)|b_{\tau}|\,R\,d\tau.

Taking the supremum over t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T] proves the lemma. ∎

Lemma A.6 (Minimum orthogonal alignment error).

For any 𝐮,𝐯∈ℝm\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{m},

(65) min𝐇∈O⁡(m)⁡‖𝐮−𝐇𝐯‖=|‖𝐮‖−‖𝐯‖|.\min_{\mathbf{H}\in O(m)}\|\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{H}\mathbf{v}\|=\bigl|\|\mathbf{u}\|-\|\mathbf{v}\|\bigr|.
Proof.

For any 𝐇∈O⁡(m)\mathbf{H}\in O(m), the inequality

(66) ‖𝐮−𝐇𝐯‖≥|‖𝐮‖−‖𝐇𝐯‖|=|‖𝐮‖−‖𝐯‖|\|\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{H}\mathbf{v}\|\geq\bigl|\|\mathbf{u}\|-\|\mathbf{H}\mathbf{v}\|\bigr|=\bigl|\|\mathbf{u}\|-\|\mathbf{v}\|\bigr|

always holds. Conversely, if 𝐮,𝐯≠0\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\neq 0, choose 𝐇∈O⁡(m)\mathbf{H}\in O(m) such that

(67) 𝐇​𝐯‖𝐯‖=𝐮‖𝐮‖.\mathbf{H}\frac{\mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{v}\|}=\frac{\mathbf{u}}{\|\mathbf{u}\|}.

Then 𝐇𝐯=(‖𝐯‖/‖𝐮‖)​𝐮\mathbf{H}\mathbf{v}=(\|\mathbf{v}\|/\|\mathbf{u}\|)\mathbf{u}, so

(68) ‖𝐮−𝐇𝐯‖=‖𝐮−‖𝐯‖‖𝐮‖​𝐮‖=|‖𝐮‖−‖𝐯‖|.\|\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{H}\mathbf{v}\|=\Bigl\|\mathbf{u}-\frac{\|\mathbf{v}\|}{\|\mathbf{u}\|}\mathbf{u}\Bigr\|=\bigl|\|\mathbf{u}\|-\|\mathbf{v}\|\bigr|.

Finally, if 𝐮=0\mathbf{u}=0 or 𝐯=0\mathbf{v}=0, the result holds trivially. ∎

A.3. A uniform high-probability bound

Building upon the deterministic trajectory decomposition provided in the previous subsection, this part gives a uniform high-probability bound for pairwise trajectory alignment proof.

Proposition A.7 (Deterministic pairwise alignment).

Suppose 𝐱t∈[0,T](1)\mathbf{x}_{t\in[0,T]}^{(1)} and 𝐱t∈[0,T](2)\mathbf{x}_{t\in[0,T]}^{(2)} are two exact PF-ODE trajectories with starting noise 𝐱T(1)\mathbf{x}_{T}^{(1)} and 𝐱T(2)\mathbf{x}_{T}^{(2)}. Then there exists 𝐇∈O⁡(d)\mathbf{H}\in O(d) such that

(69) sup0≤t≤T∥𝐃t(1)−𝐇𝐃t(2)∥≤AT|\displaystyle\sup_{0\leq t\leq T}\|\mathbf{D}_{t}^{(1)}-\mathbf{H}\mathbf{D}_{t}^{(2)}\|\leq A_{T}\bigl| ∥Q𝐱T(1)∥−∥Q𝐱T(2)∥|\displaystyle\|Q\mathbf{x}_{T}^{(1)}\|-\|Q\mathbf{x}_{T}^{(2)}\|\bigr|
+AT​(‖P​𝐱T(1)‖+‖P​𝐱T(2)‖)+2​BT​R.\displaystyle+A_{T}\bigl(\|P\mathbf{x}_{T}^{(1)}\|+\|P\mathbf{x}_{T}^{(2)}\|\bigr)+2B_{T}R.

Consequently,

(70) max0≤n≤N∥𝐃n(1)−𝐇𝐃n(2)∥≤AT|\displaystyle\max_{0\leq n\leq N}\|\mathbf{D}_{n}^{(1)}-\mathbf{H}\mathbf{D}_{n}^{(2)}\|\leq A_{T}\bigl| ∥Q𝐱T(1)∥−∥Q𝐱T(2)∥|\displaystyle\|Q\mathbf{x}_{T}^{(1)}\|-\|Q\mathbf{x}_{T}^{(2)}\|\bigr|
+AT​(‖P​𝐱T(1)‖+‖P​𝐱T(2)‖)+2​BT​R.\displaystyle+A_{T}\bigl(\|P\mathbf{x}_{T}^{(1)}\|+\|P\mathbf{x}_{T}^{(2)}\|\bigr)+2B_{T}R.
Proof.

Decompose ℝd=U⊕U⟂\mathbb{R}^{d}=U\oplus U^{\perp}. By Lemma A.6, there exists 𝐇Q∈O⁡(U⟂)\mathbf{H}_{Q}\in O(U^{\perp}) such that

(71) ‖Q​𝐱T(1)−𝐇Q​Q​𝐱T(2)‖=|‖Q​𝐱T(1)‖−‖Q​𝐱T(2)‖|.\|Q\mathbf{x}_{T}^{(1)}-\mathbf{H}_{Q}Q\mathbf{x}_{T}^{(2)}\|=\bigl|\|Q\mathbf{x}_{T}^{(1)}\|-\|Q\mathbf{x}_{T}^{(2)}\|\bigr|.

Choose any 𝐇P∈O⁡(U)\mathbf{H}_{P}\in O(U) and define

(72) 𝐇:=𝐇P⊕𝐇Q∈O⁡(d).\mathbf{H}:=\mathbf{H}_{P}\oplus\mathbf{H}_{Q}\in O(d).

By Lemma A.4,

(73) Q​𝐃t(k)=(ρt−1)​Q​𝐱T(k).Q\mathbf{D}_{t}^{(k)}=(\rho_{t}-1)Q\mathbf{x}_{T}^{(k)}.

Hence

(74) Q⁡(𝐃t(1)−𝐇𝐃t(2))=(ρt−1)​(Q​𝐱T(1)−𝐇Q​Q​𝐱T(2)),Q\bigl(\mathbf{D}_{t}^{(1)}-\mathbf{H}\mathbf{D}_{t}^{(2)}\bigr)=(\rho_{t}-1)\bigl(Q\mathbf{x}_{T}^{(1)}-\mathbf{H}_{Q}Q\mathbf{x}_{T}^{(2)}\bigr),

so

(75) sup0≤t≤T‖Q⁡(𝐃t(1)−𝐇𝐃t(2))‖≤AT​|‖Q​𝐱T(1)‖−‖Q​𝐱T(2)‖|.\sup_{0\leq t\leq T}\|Q(\mathbf{D}_{t}^{(1)}-\mathbf{H}\mathbf{D}_{t}^{(2)})\|\leq A_{T}\bigl|\|Q\mathbf{x}_{T}^{(1)}\|-\|Q\mathbf{x}_{T}^{(2)}\|\bigr|.

For the UU-component, Lemma A.5 gives

(76) ‖P⁡(𝐃t(1)−𝐇𝐃t(2))‖\displaystyle\|P(\mathbf{D}_{t}^{(1)}-\mathbf{H}\mathbf{D}_{t}^{(2)})\| ≤‖P​𝐃t(1)‖+‖P​𝐃t(2)‖\displaystyle\leq\|P\mathbf{D}_{t}^{(1)}\|+\|P\mathbf{D}_{t}^{(2)}\|
≤AT​‖P​𝐱T(1)‖+BT​R+AT|P​𝐱T(2)|+BT​R.\displaystyle\leq A_{T}\|P\mathbf{x}_{T}^{(1)}\|+B_{T}R+A_{T}\|P\mathbf{x}_{T}^{(2)}\|+B_{T}R.

Combining the UU and U⟂U^{\perp} parts via the triangle inequality proves the continuous-time bound. The discrete-time bound follows from

(77) max0≤n≤N⁡‖𝐃n(1)−𝐇𝐃n(2)‖≤sup0≤t≤T‖𝐃t(1)−𝐇𝐃t(2)‖.\max_{0\leq n\leq N}\|\mathbf{D}_{n}^{(1)}-\mathbf{H}\mathbf{D}_{n}^{(2)}\|\leq\sup_{0\leq t\leq T}\|\mathbf{D}_{t}^{(1)}-\mathbf{H}\mathbf{D}_{t}^{(2)}\|.

∎

Lemma A.8 (Gaussian norm concentration).

If 𝐠∼𝒩⁡(0,𝐈m)\mathbf{g}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I}_{m}), then for every t>0t>0,

(78) ℙ(|∥𝐠∥−𝔼∥𝐠∥|≥t)≤2e−t2/2,𝔼∥𝐠∥≤m.\mathbb{P}\bigl(|\|\mathbf{g}\|-\mathbb{E}\|\mathbf{g}\||\geq t\bigr)\leq 2e^{-t^{2}/2},\qquad\mathbb{E}\|\mathbf{g}\|\leq\sqrt{m}.
Proof.

The map 𝐠↦‖𝐠‖\mathbf{g}\mapsto\|\mathbf{g}\| is 11-Lipschitz, so the first inequality is the standard Gaussian concentration inequality. The second follows from Jensen’s inequality:

(79) 𝔼​‖𝐠‖≤𝔼​‖𝐠‖2=m.\mathbb{E}\|\mathbf{g}\|\leq\sqrt{\mathbb{E}\|\mathbf{g}\|^{2}}=\sqrt{m}.

∎

Theorem A.9 (Explicit version of Theorem 3.1).

Suppose that 𝐱T(1),…,𝐱T(M)\mathbf{x}_{T}^{(1)},\dots,\mathbf{x}_{T}^{(M)} are i.i.d. samples from the exact noised marginal pTp_{T}. Then for every δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta,

(80) max⁡inf𝐇∈O⁡(d)1≤a,b≤M⁡max0≤n≤N\displaystyle\max_{1\leq a,b\leq M}\;\inf_{\mathbf{H}\in O(d)}\max_{0\leq n\leq N} ‖𝐃n(a)−𝐇𝐃n(b)‖\displaystyle\|\mathbf{D}_{n}^{(a)}-\mathbf{H}\mathbf{D}_{n}^{(b)}\|
≤2​2​AT​νT​log⁡4​Mδ\displaystyle\leq 2\sqrt{2}\,A_{T}\nu_{T}\sqrt{\log\frac{4M}{\delta}}
+2​AT​(αT​R+νT​[r+2​log⁡2​Mδ])+2​BT​R.\displaystyle+2A_{T}\Bigl(\alpha_{T}R+\nu_{T}\Bigl[\sqrt{r}+\sqrt{2\log\frac{2M}{\delta}}\Bigr]\Bigr)+2B_{T}R.
Proof.

By Lemma A.1, the noised marginal at time TT is

(81) pT​(𝐱)=∑m=1Mπm​𝒩​(αT​𝝁m,νT2​𝐈d).p_{T}(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{m=1}^{M}\pi_{m}\mathcal{N}(\alpha_{T}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{m},\nu_{T}^{2}\mathbf{I}_{d}).

Hence each sample can be represented as

(82) 𝐱T(k)=αT​𝝁Ck+νT​𝐠(k),\mathbf{x}_{T}^{(k)}=\alpha_{T}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{C_{k}}+\nu_{T}\mathbf{g}^{(k)},

where Ck∈{1,…,M}C_{k}\in\{1,\dots,M\}, ℙ⁡(Ck=m)=πm\mathbb{P}(C_{k}=m)=\pi_{m}, and 𝐠(k)∼𝒩⁡(0,𝐈d)\mathbf{g}^{(k)}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I}_{d}). Since 𝝁Ck∈U\boldsymbol{\mu}_{C_{k}}\in U,

(83) Q​𝐱T(k)=νT​Q​𝐠(k)∼𝒩⁡(0,νT2​𝐈d−r),Q\mathbf{x}_{T}^{(k)}=\nu_{T}Q\mathbf{g}^{(k)}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\nu_{T}^{2}\mathbf{I}_{d-r}),

and

(84) P​𝐱T(k)=αT​𝝁Ck+νT​P​𝐠(k).P\mathbf{x}_{T}^{(k)}=\alpha_{T}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{C_{k}}+\nu_{T}P\mathbf{g}^{(k)}.

We first control the QQ-component. By Lemma A.8 and a union bound, with probability at least 1−δ/21-\delta/2,

(85) max1≤k≤M⁡|‖Q​𝐱T(k)‖−𝔼​‖Q​𝐱T(k)‖|≤νT​2​log⁡4​Mδ.\max_{1\leq k\leq M}\Bigl|\|Q\mathbf{x}_{T}^{(k)}\|-\mathbb{E}\|Q\mathbf{x}_{T}^{(k)}\|\Bigr|\leq\nu_{T}\sqrt{2\log\frac{4M}{\delta}}.

Therefore, on this event,

(86) max1≤a,b≤M⁡|‖Q​𝐱T(a)‖−‖Q​𝐱T(b)‖|≤2​νT​2​log⁡4​Mδ.\max_{1\leq a,b\leq M}\bigl|\|Q\mathbf{x}_{T}^{(a)}\|-\|Q\mathbf{x}_{T}^{(b)}\|\bigr|\leq 2\nu_{T}\sqrt{2\log\frac{4M}{\delta}}.

Next we control the PP-component. Since P​𝐠(k)∼𝒩⁡(0,𝐈r)P\mathbf{g}^{(k)}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I}_{r}) on UU, Lemma A.8 and ‖𝝁Ck‖≤R\|\boldsymbol{\mu}_{C_{k}}\|\leq R imply that, with probability at least 1−δ/21-\delta/2,

(87) max1≤k≤M⁡‖P​𝐱T(k)‖≤αT​R+νT​(r+2​log⁡2​Mδ).\max_{1\leq k\leq M}\|P\mathbf{x}_{T}^{(k)}\|\leq\alpha_{T}R+\nu_{T}\Bigl(\sqrt{r}+\sqrt{2\log\frac{2M}{\delta}}\Bigr).

On the intersection of these two events, whose probability is at least 1−δ1-\delta, Proposition A.7 gives, for every pair (a,b)(a,b), some orthogonal matrix 𝐇a,b∈O⁡(d)\mathbf{H}_{a,b}\in O(d) such that

(88) max0≤n≤N|𝐃n(a)\displaystyle\max_{0\leq n\leq N}\|\mathbf{D}_{n}^{(a)} −𝐇a,b𝐃n(b)∥\displaystyle-\mathbf{H}_{a,b}\mathbf{D}_{n}^{(b)}\|
≤AT⋅2​νT​2​log⁡4​Mδ\displaystyle\leq A_{T}\cdot 2\nu_{T}\sqrt{2\log\frac{4M}{\delta}}
+AT⋅2(αTR+νT[r+2​log⁡2​Mδ])+2BTR.\displaystyle+A_{T}\cdot 2\Bigl(\alpha_{T}R+\nu_{T}\Bigl[\sqrt{r}+\sqrt{2\log\frac{2M}{\delta}}\Bigr]\Bigr)+2B_{T}R.

Taking the maximum over (a,b)(a,b) and then the infimum over 𝐇∈O⁡(d)\mathbf{H}\in O(d) yields the stated inequality. ∎

Proof of Corollary 3.2.

Divide the bound in Theorem A.9 by νT​d\nu_{T}\sqrt{d}. This gives

(89) 1νT​dmax1≤a,b≤ninf𝐇∈O⁡(d)\displaystyle\frac{1}{\nu_{T}\sqrt{d}}\max_{1\leq a,b\leq n}\inf_{\mathbf{H}\in O(d)} max0≤ℓ≤L⁡‖𝐃ℓ(a)−𝐇𝐃ℓ(b)‖\displaystyle\max_{0\leq\ell\leq L}\|\mathbf{D}_{\ell}^{(a)}-\mathbf{H}\mathbf{D}_{\ell}^{(b)}\|
≤2​2​AT​log⁡(4​M/δ)d+2​AT​rd\displaystyle\leq 2\sqrt{2}\,A_{T}\sqrt{\frac{\log(4M/\delta)}{d}}+2A_{T}\sqrt{\frac{r}{d}}
+2​AT​2​log⁡(2​M/δ)d+2​AT​αT​RνT​d+2​BT​RνT​d.\displaystyle+2A_{T}\sqrt{\frac{2\log(2M/\delta)}{d}}+2A_{T}\frac{\alpha_{T}R}{\nu_{T}\sqrt{d}}+2B_{T}\frac{R}{\nu_{T}\sqrt{d}}.

Since r+log⁡n=o⁡(d)r+\log n=o(d) and R=o⁡(νT​d)R=o(\nu_{T}\sqrt{d}), the right-hand side converges to 00 for every fixed δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1). This proves the claim. ∎

A.4. Proofs of the low-dimensionality Corollary

We now show that under mild assumptions, each PF-ODE trajectory is confined to a low-dimensional subspace. Moreover, a simple alignment brings all trajectories into a single shared subspace.

Corollary A.10 (Explicit version of Corollary 3.3).

Suppose 𝐱t∈[0,T](k)\mathbf{x}_{t\in[0,T]}^{(k)} is an exact PF-ODE trajectory. Then

(90) 𝐱t(k)∈𝒮k:=U⊕span⁡{Q​𝐱T(k)},∀t∈[0,T].\mathbf{x}_{t}^{(k)}\in\mathcal{S}_{k}:=U\oplus\operatorname{span}\{Q\mathbf{x}_{T}^{(k)}\},\qquad\forall t\in[0,T].

In particular,

(91) dim(𝒮k)≤r+1.\dim(\mathcal{S}_{k})\leq r+1.

Hence, on any discrete reverse-time grid T=t0>t1>⋯>tL=0T=t_{0}>t_{1}>\cdots>t_{L}=0, the trajectory matrix

(92) 𝐗(k)∈ℝ(L+1)×d,rowℓ​(𝐗(k))=(𝐱ℓ(k))⊤,\mathbf{X}^{(k)}\in\mathbb{R}^{(L+1)\times d},\qquad\text{row}_{\ell}(\mathbf{X}^{(k)})=(\mathbf{x}_{\ell}^{(k)})^{\top},

satisfies

(93) rank⁡(𝐗(k))≤r+1.\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{X}^{(k)})\leq r+1.

Equivalently, the empirical trajectory covariance

(94) 𝚺traj(k):=1M+1​∑m=0M(𝐱ℓ(k)−𝐱¯(k))​(𝐱ℓ(k)−𝐱¯(k))⊤\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{traj}}^{(k)}:=\frac{1}{M+1}\sum_{m=0}^{M}\bigl(\mathbf{x}_{\ell}^{(k)}-\bar{\mathbf{x}}^{(k)}\bigr)\bigl(\mathbf{x}_{\ell}^{(k)}-\bar{\mathbf{x}}^{(k)}\bigr)^{\top}

has rank at most r+1r+1, and therefore

(95) λj​(𝚺traj(k))=0,j≥r+2.\lambda_{j}\!\left(\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{traj}}^{(k)}\right)=0,\qquad j\geq r+2.
Proof.

By Lemma A.4,

(96) Q​𝐱t(k)=ρt​Q​𝐱T(k),Q\mathbf{x}_{t}^{(k)}=\rho_{t}Q\mathbf{x}_{T}^{(k)},

which lies in the one-dimensional subspace span⁡{Q​𝐱T(k)}\operatorname{span}\{Q\mathbf{x}_{T}^{(k)}\}. On the other hand,

(97) P​𝐱t(k)∈UP\mathbf{x}_{t}^{(k)}\in U

for all t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T]. Therefore,

(98) 𝐱t(k)=P​𝐱t(k)+Q​𝐱t(k)∈U⊕span⁡{Q​𝐱T(k)}.\mathbf{x}_{t}^{(k)}=P\mathbf{x}_{t}^{(k)}+Q\mathbf{x}_{t}^{(k)}\in U\oplus\operatorname{span}\{Q\mathbf{x}_{T}^{(k)}\}.

This proves that the whole trajectory lies in the linear subspace 𝒮k\mathcal{S}_{k} with dim(𝒮k)≤r+1\dim(\mathcal{S}_{k})\leq r+1. Since every row of 𝐗(k)\mathbf{X}^{(k)} belongs to 𝒮k\mathcal{S}_{k}, we have

(99) rank⁡(𝐗(k))≤dim(𝒮k)≤r+1.\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{X}^{(k)})\leq\dim(\mathcal{S}_{k})\leq r+1.

Since 𝒮k\mathcal{S}_{k} is a linear subspace, it contains the centered trajectory vectors. Thus, the image of the covariance matrix 𝚺traj(k)\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{traj}}^{(k)} lies within 𝒮k\mathcal{S}_{k}, implying

(100) rank⁡(𝚺traj(k))≤r+1.\operatorname{rank}\!\left(\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{traj}}^{(k)}\right)\leq r+1.

This directly leads to the conclusion about the eigenvalues. ∎

Corollary A.11 (Explicit version of Corollary 3.4).

Fix any unit vector 𝐞∈U⟂\mathbf{e}\in U^{\perp}. For each trajectory kk, choose an orthogonal matrix 𝐇k∈O⁡(d)\mathbf{H}_{k}\in O(d) such that

(101) 𝐇k|U=𝐈,𝐇k​Q​𝐱T(k)=‖Q​𝐱T(k)‖​𝐞.\mathbf{H}_{k}|_{U}=\mathbf{I},\qquad\mathbf{H}_{k}Q\mathbf{x}_{T}^{(k)}=\|Q\mathbf{x}_{T}^{(k)}\|\,\mathbf{e}.

Define the aligned trajectory

(102) 𝐱~t(k):=𝐇k​𝐱t(k).\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{t}^{(k)}:=\mathbf{H}_{k}\mathbf{x}_{t}^{(k)}.

Then

(103) 𝐱~t(k)∈𝒮~:=U⊕span⁡{𝐞},∀k,∀t∈[0,T].\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{t}^{(k)}\in\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}:=U\oplus\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf{e}\},\qquad\forall k,\ \forall t\in[0,T].

In particular,

(104) dim(𝒮~)≤r+1.\dim(\widetilde{\mathcal{S}})\leq r+1.

Hence, if 𝐗~∈ℝn⁡(L+1)×d\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n(L+1)\times d} denotes the pooled aligned trajectory matrix obtained by stacking all aligned trajectory states, then

(105) rank⁡(𝐗~)≤r+1.\operatorname{rank}(\widetilde{\mathbf{X}})\leq r+1.

Equivalently, the pooled covariance of the aligned trajectories has rank at most r+1r+1.

Proof.

By construction, 𝐇k\mathbf{H}_{k} acts as the identity on UU. Therefore, since P​𝐱t(k)∈UP\mathbf{x}_{t}^{(k)}\in U,

(106) 𝐇k​P​𝐱t(k)=P​𝐱t(k)∈U.\mathbf{H}_{k}P\mathbf{x}_{t}^{(k)}=P\mathbf{x}_{t}^{(k)}\in U.

Moreover, using Lemma A.4,

(107) Q​𝐱t(k)=ρt​Q​𝐱T(k),Q\mathbf{x}_{t}^{(k)}=\rho_{t}Q\mathbf{x}_{T}^{(k)},

and thus

(108) 𝐇k​Q​𝐱t(k)=ρt​𝐇k​Q​𝐱T(k)=ρt​‖Q​𝐱T(k)‖​𝐞∈span⁡{𝐞}.\mathbf{H}_{k}Q\mathbf{x}_{t}^{(k)}=\rho_{t}\mathbf{H}_{k}Q\mathbf{x}_{T}^{(k)}=\rho_{t}\|Q\mathbf{x}_{T}^{(k)}\|\,\mathbf{e}\in\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf{e}\}.

Combining the UU-part and the U⟂U^{\perp}-part gives

(109) 𝐱~t(k)=𝐇k​𝐱t(k)∈U⊕span⁡{𝐞}=𝒮~.\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{t}^{(k)}=\mathbf{H}_{k}\mathbf{x}_{t}^{(k)}\in U\oplus\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf{e}\}=\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}.

Therefore all aligned trajectories share a single subspace 𝒮~\widetilde{\mathcal{S}} of dimension at most r+1r+1, which immediately yields the rank results. ∎

Remark 1 (Connection to least-squares reconstruction).

The above corollaries provide a direct explanation for the least-squares residual observed in practice. Specifically, every state 𝐱n(k)\mathbf{x}^{(k)}_{n} on a given trajectory kk belongs to the same linear subspace 𝒮k\mathcal{S}_{k} with

(110) dim(𝒮k)≤r+1.\dim(\mathcal{S}_{k})\leq r+1.

Therefore, if a history buffer

(111) {𝐱n−B(k),𝐱n−B+1(k),…,𝐱n−1(k)}\{\mathbf{x}_{n-B}^{(k)},\mathbf{x}_{n-B+1}^{(k)},\dots,\mathbf{x}_{n-1}^{(k)}\}

spans 𝒮k\mathcal{S}_{k}, then the least-squares reconstruction error of 𝐱n(k)\mathbf{x}_{n}^{(k)} from this buffer is exactly zero:

(112) min𝐜∈ℝB⁡‖𝐱n(k)−∑j=1Bcj​𝐱n−j(k)‖=0.\min_{\mathbf{c}\in\mathbb{R}^{B}}\left\|\mathbf{x}_{n}^{(k)}-\sum_{j=1}^{B}c_{j}\mathbf{x}_{n-j}^{(k)}\right\|=0.

Thus, in the exact spherical GMM setting, a sufficiently rich short buffer already determines the future point by linear regression. In realistic diffusion models we do not expect this identity to hold exactly, but small least-squares residuals strongly suggest that the denoising dynamics remain approximately low-dimensional.

Appendix B Experimental Results

B.1. Ablation Study

B.1.1. Compatibility with Different Base Solvers.

To further evaluate the robustness and generalization ability of LEAP, we conduct an additional ablation experiment by integrating LEAP with various widely used ODE solvers, including Euler, DPM++, iPNDM, and UniPC. This experiment is conducted on SD3.5 with NFE=1515 and r=5r=5. As shown in Table 3, LEAP improves human preference and text-image alignment metrics (HPSv2, ImageReward, and CLIPScore) across all tested baseline solvers.
